paper_title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360$^{\circ}$ View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360$^{\circ}$ scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360$^{\circ}$ panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. The four stages follow what photographer actually does upon arriving at scene: look around, settle on direction, adjust the frame, and press the shutter. (1) Given 360 panorama, the system scans look directions and (2) scores each using the proposed four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Integrity, and Aesthetics. The maximum fixes the camera direction. (3) The frame is then refined within that view, and (4) the final photograph is rendered natively from the panorama. The same four tokens also ground the explanation: our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to cite these tokens and conditioned on their measured assessments. Below, two results show the selected crop and the produced explanation; phrases grounded in the four assessments are highlighted.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: While computational photography has effectively matured low-level image acquisition (Mohammadi et al., 2026; Brooks et al., 2019; Lee & Ding, 2024; Zhang et al., 2021b; He et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; Feijoo et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2024; 2026a;b), higher-level compositional choices require separate treatment. When cropping an image, photographer answers four fundamental questions: what the subject is, where to place it, whether critical elements are cut off , and if the overall composition is visually appealing. These four independent judgments are susceptible to distinct failures, such as selecting correct subject with poor placement. Furthermore, panoramic framing introduces an earlier decision: determining direction before the frame is formed. Existing 2D cropping methods assume that the input is already pre-shot photograph. Our goal is to combine composition-based direction selection with refined framing, camera-parameter output, and measurement-conditioned explanations. PhotoGuider evaluates candidate crops using four interpretable photographic tokens: Subject (S), Composition (C), Integrity (I), and Aesthetics (A). These assessments collectively score panoramic view directions, rank candidate frames, guide spatial refinements, and anchor MLLM explanations in concrete measurements. Pre-trained vision models extract the features, and compact scorers learn to combine them for framing decisions. This architecture offers three advantages. First, interpretability is structural at the feature level and post hoc at the attribution level. Second, the trainable decision layer has limited capacity to reduce the risk of overfitting to dataset-specific biases. Third, it natively generalizes to full panoramas, as the tokens evaluate intrinsic geometry and semantics on perspective projections. The overview of PhotoGuider is demonstrated in Fig. 1. Overall, PhotoGuider provides three contributions: Composition-Aware Cropping: The decision layer selects the optimal box using four photographic tokens and learned compact rankers with only 63k parameters, achieving competitive performance across two benchmarks while confining the MLLM to bounded consultant role that neither scores nor makes decisions. Measurement-Conditioned Explanations: We condition fine-tuned MLLM on the token assessments and geometric measurements, allowing its measurement-based statements to be checked against the supplied values. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first system for automatic composition-aware framing from 360 panoramas that combines explicit view-level direction selection with cameraparameter output for re-rendering and measurement-conditioned explanations based on shared photographic feature groups.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Image Cropping. Early croppers optimize hand-designed saliency and composition energies (Nishiyama et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016). Generate-and-rank methods score candidate boxes using expert edits, professional photographs, saliency partitioning, or reinforcement learning (Yan et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2017b; Wei et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2024; Wang & Shen, 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; 2019; Hamara & Freeman, 2025). End-to-end methods directly regress crops using cascaded regression, grid anchors, score maps, meta-learning, or set prediction (Guo et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2019; 2022; Tu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a; Jia et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a; Pan et al., 2024; 2023), often incorporating relational, boundaryaware, subject-aware, or synthesized composition signals (Li et al., 2020b; Hong et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025; Wong & Wong, 2025; Zhang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024; Su et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025). Their fixed objectives make the scoring evidence difficult to inspect. MLLM-based croppers use vision-language priors and fine-tuning or prompting for aesthetic reasoning, increasingly producing rationales, composition categories, or capture-time guidance alongside boxes (Zhong et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Jiang & Chen, 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Viriyavisuthisakul et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026; You et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Photographic reasoning remains challenging for MLLMs (Fang & Chen, 2025). PhotoGuider generates candidates from self-supervised attention (Caron et al., 2021; Simeoni et al., 2026) and ranks them through four photographic tokens with explicitly learned weights. Its MLLM consultant makes bounded proposals, aggregated following the principle of self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022). 2 Preprint. Under review. Figure 2: One set of photographic tokens, three uses. Each token yields one assessment score for given frame, allowing the decision layers output to be separated into four interpretable metrics. These drive our entire pipeline by (1) scoring all view directions in 360 scene, (2) ranking shortlisted framings and gating each refinement step, and (3) anchoring the fine-tuned MLLMs explanations. An optional generalist MLLM acts only as consultant during refinement. Aesthetic Assessment and Explainable Critique. Aesthetic scoring has progressed from regressors trained on crowd-rated photographs (Murray et al., 2012; Talebi & Milanfar, 2018; He et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024a) to CLIPand LMM-based models (Wang et al., 2023b; Ke et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). Composition datasets annotate thirds, symmetry, and triangles (Lee et al., 2018a; Zhang et al., 2021a; Zhao et al., 2025), providing reasoning priors for VLM croppers (Dong et al., 2026). Early critique generation used photographers comments (Chang et al., 2017). MLLMs generate aesthetic critiques at scale (Huang et al., 2024c;b; Zhou et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025), assess quality through reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2025b), or use interpretable concept subspaces (Liu & Wagemans, 2026). Their free-form rationales receive limited checks against measurable image properties, raising concerns about hallucination and faithfulness (Li et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2024; Jacovi & Goldberg, 2020). PhotoGuider uses aesthetic predictions and composition measurements as token inputs and filters explainer training drafts against these measurements, following rationale-distillation approach akin to rejection sampling (Zelikman et al., 2022; Hsieh et al., 2023). View Selection in 360 Scenes. Prior work extracts normal-field-of-view trajectories from panoramic video using learned videography, piloting agents, hyperlapse, highlight ranking, summarization, or saliency-guided camera paths (Su et al., 2016; Su & Grauman, 2017; Hu et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018b; Kang & Cho, 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2024). Other work optimizes projection, snap angles, or capture guidance (Kim et al., 2017; Xiong & Grauman, 2018; Rao et al., 2022; Su et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025a), predicts 360 viewer attention (Rai et al., 2017; Sitzmann et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018), or steers real and reconstructed cameras with aesthetic rewards (Fang & Zhang, 2017; Xiong et al., 2017; AlZayer et al., 2021; Limoyo et al., 2024; Uchida et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Jiang & Chen, 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Saliency alone is insufficient for aesthetic view selection (Chen et al., 2024), and existing view scores lack interpretability or conflate framing with camera-pose objectives. PhotoGuider uses the same 60 measurements in LightGBM framing ranker and an additive direction scorer. It selects direction, reprojects the view, and refines the crop, with shared measurements supporting view selection, ranking, and explanation. Interpretable Decision Layers. Generalized additive models provide per-feature contributions by construction, including boosted GA2Ms, explainable boosting machines (Lou et al., 2013; Nori et al., 2019), and neural variants (Agarwal et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2021; Radenovic et al., 2022). Gradient-boosted trees perform well on tabular data (Ke et al., 2017; Grinsztajn et al., 2022), support 3 Preprint. Under review. Figure 3: The three learned components of PhotoGuider. We use single ground-truth crops from FCDB and top-rated crops from GAICD, with labels defined by the overlap (IoU) between candidate framings and reference crops. (1) Ranker. Candidates are scored using four LightGBM models (two regression and two ranking) operating on two feature tiers: 17D core set (saliency, geometry) and 60D full set (adding SAM object semantics, aesthetic scores, and CLIP prompts). Blending these model outputs yields three quality scores (qA, qB, qC) to determine the optimal crop. (2) Refinement Gates. Six LightGBM gates adjust the selected crop by predicting IoU gains: one gate recenters the frame (via rule-of-thirds and CLIP-attention), four evaluate expansion (based on subject coverage, composition, scale-aesthetic variance, and golden ratio alignment), and final gate shrinks the frame if no expansion triggers. (3) Explainer MLLM. It generates explanations conditioned on the crop, measured geometry, and ranker attributions. Training data drafts are filtered via four strict quality checks (unmasked geometry, numerical consistency, feature citations, and vocabulary validity). LambdaRank objectives (Burges, 2010), and admit isotonic calibration (Zadrozny & Elkan, 2002; Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana, 2005). PhotoGuider uses token-grouped neural additive view scorer with pairwise terms and calibrated LightGBM ranker and gates. TreeSHAP (Lundberg et al., 2020) provides ranker attributions, with secant approximation for the calibrated head (Appendix A.1).

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: 3.1 OVERVIEW photographer arriving at scene acts in four steps: decide which way to point the camera, compose the shot, polish it, and, when possible, ask second pair of eyes. PhotoGuider performs these steps as follows: Stage (a) extends the 2D cropper into complete 360 framing system by scoring candidate look directions across the panorama using shared assessments and reprojecting the optimal direction into working view (Sec. 3.7). Stage (b) generates, filters, and ranks candidate framings to select top proposal (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3). Stage (c) applies spatial adjustments when predicted beneficial by learned gate (Sec. 3.4). Together, stages (b) and (c) constitute the fast mode, and the full mode further incorporates stage (d), which consults specialized MLLM within bounded constraints (Sec. 3.5). Finally, composition-aware explanations are derived from the same assessments (Sec. 3.6). The method and training overviews are shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3, respectively. Integrity is quantified via geometric and boundary statistics relating the segmented objects and subject mask to the crop border. Aesthetics is predicted using two learned aesthetic assessment models, LAION (Schuhmann et al., 2022) and FGAesQ (Yang et al., 2026b). Figure 4 illustrates the four tokens. Each description below states what token measures; the definitions of every feature are provided in Appendix A.1. Subject (10D). Evaluates focal attention and object completeness using three models: DINOv3 attention captures focal strength (3D), InSPyReNet saliency quantifies subject coverage and prominence (2D), and SAM provides frame coverage, spatial placement, and cross-model agreement with InSPyReNet (4D), supplemented by subject scale (1D). Integrity (20D). Measures information preservation and structural disruption using SAM-derived representation. Encoder features (9D) quantify visual information density, object signal distribution, crop-versus-background contrast, whole-image baseline, and shot scale. Decoder features (11D) capture object-level composition, including object count, dominant area shares, size disparity, boundary containment cleanliness, edge margins, and depth layering. Composition (22D). Spatial layout is parameterized across three sources: saliency geometry (10D) covering rule-of-thirds, symmetry, triangles, balance, offset, tightness, and aspect ratio; SAM object parsing (3D) evaluating grid alignment and center-versus-thirds bias; and CLIP features (9D) measuring eight canonical cues plus peak match score. The first pair uses the 17-dimensional core compositional set (the saliency measures of Subject, the geometric rules of Composition, and one color term). Its regression and ranking outputs are combined with two sets of weights to obtain qA and qB. The second pair uses the full 60-dimensional set, applies isotonic calibration to its regression head, and produces qC. Each component is min-max normalized within the image. Pool-relative features are computed over all ten boxes and then frozen; normalization and the arg max run on K3. Token attributions are exact for three uncalibrated heads carrying combined weight of 0.88; the calibrated head (weight 0.12) uses secant approximation (Appendix A.1). 3.4 GATED REFINEMENT Three sequential spatial moves adjust the chosen frame into the refined frame b. Each move is gated by LightGBM regressor predicting the expected IoU gain on the current image, firing only when the predicted gain exceeds dedicated threshold. In the recenter stage, two center targets compete for alignment: tthirds, representing the saliency centroid aligned with the nearest rule-ofthirds point, and tcam, representing the centroid of CLIP compositional attention. The gate predicts the IoU advantage ˆm of the CLIP target, computes weight = clip( ˆm/Tg, 0, 1), and shifts the frame center by fraction β toward = (1 w)tthirds + wtcam. In the Expand stage, four independent gates evaluate the gain ˆgk(s) of enlarging the frame by scale factor centered at fixed ratio. Each gate assesses distinct signal: subject coverage, CLIP wide-versus-tight response, aesthetic score variation under enlargement, and subject proximity to the nearest goldensection point. gate fires when maxs ˆgk(s) > τe, and the frame adopts the scale factor providing the highest predicted gain among all fired gates. Perspective views are reprojected on an overlapping grid of pan and tilt angles, and the same 60 features are extracted for each view exactly as for crop. An additive view scorer maps the features of view to composition score. It is trained on the GAICD (Zeng et al., 2022) training set, whose mean opinion scores rate candidate frames. The scoring model is token-grouped neural additive network whose output is the sum of four token-specific summands, attributing the strength of each candidate direction to its constituent tokens. The direction with the highest aggregate score is selected as the optimal view. Fine: framing in the chosen direction. The selected direction is reprojected into wider working view, which then enters the cropping pipeline described in Secs. 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, and 3.5. The resulting box is converted through the working views pinhole model into camera parameters, pan, tilt, field of view and aspect ratio, and the photograph is re-rendered from the panorama at full resolution.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 DATASETS AND METRICS Following the protocol of Cropper (Lee et al., 2025) and Venus (Du et al., 2026), we evaluate PhotoGuider across two cropping benchmarks: the FCDB testing set (348 images) for aspect ratio-aware cropping, and FLMS (500 images) for free-form cropping. Training samples are collected from the FCDB training set with single ground-truth crops (1395 images) and GAICD with top-rated crops (1000 images). We report the mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) and the boundary displacement error (BDE). Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.5. 4.2 COMPARISON WITH BASELINES We compare the 2D cropping performance of PhotoGuider on the FCDB and FLMS datasets against state-of-the-art baselines, including DIC (Wang & Shen, 2017), DIC (Wang et al., 2019), A2RL (Li et al., 2018), A3RL (Li et al., 2019), VPN (Wei et al., 2018), CACNet (Hong et al., 2021), GAIC (Zeng et al., 2022), CAGR (Zhu et al., 2025), InstructCrop (Sheng et al., 2025), Cropper (Lee et al., 2025), and Venus (Du et al., 2026). We collected 100 panoramic scenes from the Poly Haven library, covering diverse indoor and outdoor environments across both day and night conditions. We compare PhotoGuider (fast mode) against CACNet (Hong et al., 2021), an end-to-end deep cropper, and Venus (Du et al., 2026), an MLLM-based cropper. All methods follow an identical two-stage protocol using their respective scoring mechanisms. CACNet uses the maximum confidence score from its composition classifier, whereas Venus relies on its composition score (110 scale) decoded greedily with fixed seed. The top-scoring view establishes the primary direction, after which each method crops its corresponding 60 working view. The resulting bounding boxes are converted to camera parameters and re-rendered from the panorama. None of the three methods is trained on panoramas. Participants ranked the three anonymized framings for each scene in randomized order. The participants provided 4,820 rankings. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: PhotoGuider models photographers framing process using four interpretable photographic tokens. These tokens drive compact ranker for candidate selection, gated refinement module, and an explainer providing grounded rationales. PhotoGuider achieves competitive performance across two benchmarks and, to our knowledge, is the first method to combine explicit compositionbased direction selection in 360 panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output, and measurement-conditioned explanations. User evaluations show clear preference for our crops over end-to-end and MLLM baselines. PhotoGuider combines view selection, crop refinement, and measurement-conditioned explanations in one pipeline. Limitations. Framing adjustments rely on discrete step fractions, approximating targets falling between sampled intervals. Also, view selection uses single argmax, returning one frame even in scenes with multiple strong regions regardless of user preference. Future work will examine continuous refinement and user-guided view selection. 9 Preprint. Under review.

sections.content: This document provides supplementary material for the paper PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360 View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments to complement the main manuscript. Sec. A.1, A.2, A.3, and A.4 provide details of the photographic tokens, refinement gates, MLLM consultant, and Explainer, respectively. Sec. A.5 offers implementation details of PhotoGuider. Sec. A.6 provides the ablation study of modules in the refinement stage. Sec. A.7 gives the detailed analysis of user preferences for 360 framings. 19 Preprint. Under review. project (https://ntuneillee.github.io/ Supplementary material. The page research/photoguider/) provides two videos of the full 360 pipeline, from direction search to the final native re-render with its explanation, and the ten user-study scenes in which our framing was preferred most strongly, each showing the panorama, the three methods framings with their first-place shares and camera parameters, our four token assessments, and the three direction fields. All scenes are CC0 panoramas from Poly Haven. A.1 THE FOUR PHOTOGRAPHIC TOKENS Shared photographic features. We measure 60 features on each perspective frame and group them into four photographic tokens: Subject (S), Composition (C), Aesthetics (A), and Integrity (I). The same feature groups support direction selection, crop ranking, and explanation. Figure 7 shows differences in token contributions between crops selected on FCDB and FLMS. We evaluate transfer across these benchmarks using the same trained checkpoint (Sec. 4.2). Subject: what is being photographed. photographer first checks whether the subject is fully in frame and how much of the frame it occupies. We measure this from three complementary views. The self-supervised attention of DINOv3 supplies saliency coverage and peak (vmix max, v1 max, v1 cov). InSPyReNet supplies the subjects precise outline and completeness (inspy capture, inspy max). The SAM object mask corresponding to the subject supplies its area share, centering, and agreement with the InSPyReNet reading (sam mask area ratio, sam mask centered x/y, sam mask vs inspy iou), the last being measure of how far two subject readings agree. geometric term completes the group with subject size (subject size ratio). Figure 7: Dataset Bias from FCDB and FLMS datasets. Each point is one crop selected by PhotoGuider, positioned by the contributions of two of the four photographic tokens. Normalized by the pooled standard deviation, the median-to-median displacement is 0.34 SD in the S-A plane and 0.47 SD in the C-I plane. Composition: how the subject is placed. With the the subject in frame, photographer checks placement against textbook vocabulary: rule of thirds, symmetry, triangular structure, balance of visual weight, negative space and shot scale. Three signals are complementary. Geometry encodes the rules directly (thirds align, sym diff, sym diag diff, tri top apex, tri bot apex, visual weight x/y, ca dist, area ratio, log aspect diff). SAM thirds alignment measures how segmented objects align with the rule-of-thirds structure (sam thirds mean/max, sam thirds vs center). CLIP multi-prompt similarity (clip sim {pro, balanced, leading, thirds, symmetric, negspace, centered, dynamic}, clip max sim) provides computable linguistic anchor for the vocabulary itself: eight prompts are eight rules stated in natural language, and CLIPs image-text alignment turns does this look like leading-lines composition into measurable number. Integrity: what the frame cut off. Last comes the reflex check of professional: the crop must not sever hand or head, must not leave mutilated object, and must keep the depth layering clean. This check evaluates object boundaries throughout the frame, independently of subject identity. That is SAMs most direct use, and all 20 dimensions of this token come from it. Encoder-side embedding statistics (sam emb norm/var/kurt, sam cand norm mean/max/std, sam cand to outside ratio, sam image total norm) characterize how much information the crop holds and how it contrasts with what lies outside; sam cos to image is continuous measure of shot scale, from close-up to full view. On the decoder side we count the objects (sam obj count in cand, sam obj top1 share, sam obj top3 share, sam obj area cv, sam dominant ratio), check whether each remains cleanly definable (sam mask mean/std/margin, whose quality and boundary margin drop when cropping line severs an object), and read the scenes depth layering (sam area cv, sam iou top12, sam cand match max). The Aesthetics token measures visual appeal using two complementary aesthetic priors. The LAION aesthetic head (laion score, laion pi minmax) represents crowds sense that an image is appealing, and FGAesQ (fgaesq score) represents fine-grained expert judgment of where the appeal lies; colour saturation (color sat mean) supplements them. The last group measures the subject-to-background separation in colour and tone that SAMs parse makes computable (sam fg bg sat diff, sam fg bg val diff, sam fg bg lab dist, sam fg var). What photographer calls the subject popping out is, concretely, contrast in saturation, value and Lab colour between foreground object and its background, and computing it requires that object to have been separated first. Token Assessments. The ranker operates as gradient-boosted tree model explained post hoc. For given frame, TreeSHAP Lundberg et al. (2020) decomposes each models raw output into feature attributions. These attributions pass through the same per-image normalization and model-output weighting as the final score, giving the approximate decomposition (cid:88) g{S,C,A,I} Φg + const, Φg = (cid:88) jFg ϕj, (3) where ϕj is the weighted attribution of feature and Fg is the disjoint index set of token g. The attribution decomposition is exact for three uncalibrated heads carrying combined weight of 0.88. For the calibrated head, which carries the remaining weight of 0.12, attributions are propagated through the isotonic mapping using secant approximation. Token attributions aggregate the feature-level shares of cross-token interactions, subject to this approximation. Finally, each Φg is mapped to percentile rank against the training reference distribution and reported independently, without any additive assumption. Candidate Generation. With target ratio, about 300 candidates come from eight sources: base geometric grid re-aspected to the ratio; anchors on the subject mask and on the top saliency peaks, each crossed with seven medium areas; multi-scale pass over the best-covering candidates; and four composition-principle generators (diagonal, negative space, leading line, boundary). Without ratio, grid of seven scales and 36 positions is laid over each of eight ratios, the seven standard ratios 16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, 2:3 and 9:16 plus the source images own ratio, deduplicated within 2%. The eight sources are described in Table.4. A.2 GATED REFINEMENT The refinement stage applies gated spatial adjustments to the selected frame to obtain b. Each adjustment is evaluated by LightGBM model that predicts its IoU gain on the current image. The adjustment is applied when the predicted gain exceeds the corresponding threshold. Recenter. The gate chooses where to place the frame center. Two candidate targets are available: tthirds, the saliency centroid softly aligned to the nearest rule-of-thirds point, and tcam, the centroid of CLIPs compositional attention. The gate predicts ˆm, the IoU advantage of the CLIP target over 21 Preprint. Under review. the thirds target, and turns it into mixing weight = clip( ˆm/Tg, 0, 1), where Tg is fixed scale constant. The target is the mix = (1 w) tthirds + tcam, and the center of the frame moves fixed fraction β of the way toward it. Expand. Four independent gates {cov, incl, aes, gold} each predict the IoU gain ˆgk(s) of enlarging the frame by factor about its centre, at fixed aspect ratio. They read four different signals: the coverage gate reads how much of the subjects saliency the current frame captures; the inclination gate reads CLIPs relative response to wide versus tight composition prompts; the -aesthetics gate reads the change of the LAION and FGAesQ scores between the current frame and the enlarged one; the -golden gate reads the change in the subjects distance to the nearest golden-section point. gate fires when maxs ˆgk(s) > τe, and the frame is enlarged to the factor with the largest predicted gain among the gates that fired. The two gates use score changes across scales. In our measurements, static scores provide little signal for expansion. We hypothesize that using score changes contributes to cross-dataset transfer. Each of the four gates evaluates distinct signal and applies its own expansion criterion. Shrink. When no expand gate fires, one fallback gate reads the shot-scale measure (the cosine between the frames SAM embedding and the whole images) and, above its own threshold τs, tightens by factor Sshr frame that looks too much like the whole image. A.3 MLLM AS CONSULTANT In the final stage, we incorporate Venus Du et al. (2026) as an MLLM consultant to propose candidate boxes, restricting it from directly scoring or making final decisions in our pipeline. Self-Consistency. primary prompt is decoded 1 + times (one greedy decoding alongside temperature-sampled outputs with fixed seeds), where the coordinate-wise median yields the core opinion vc. To build broader opinion vf , we compute the median across the union of responses from paraphrased prompts (decoded greedily with whole-image predictions filtered out). The coordinate-wise median aggregates the decoded box predictions. Twin Candidates. For each shortlist candidate ci that aligns with the consultant, defined by IoU(ci, vc) 0.5, we construct twin candidate ct i. Its center and area are shifted toward vc within fixed bounds at constant ratio, followed by complete recomputation of all 60 features. The frozen ranker then evaluates both the original and twin candidates on the merged pool, switching to the twin only when substantial margin is achieved. Bounded Concession. Prior to final delivery, if the refined box agrees with the broader opinion (IoU(b, vf ) τ ), the system interpolates the center linearly and the area geometrically: xˆb = (1 λc)xb + λcxvf , Aˆb = A1λa Aλa vf . (4) The log aspect ratio is adjusted via λr: setting λr = 0 when fixed target ratio is specified (preserving the output ratio), or λr = 1 when unconstrained, thereby adopting the consultants aspect ratio opinion to refine the discrete enumeration from the main papers Candidate generation and shortlisting section. Below the threshold τ , the consultant is considered to be proposing distinct photographic composition, and no adjustments are adopted. All hyper-parameters are fitted on the training split under bounded-regression constraint without per-image learned decisions. A.4 EXPLANATION Measurements as Shared Foundation. Our explainer cites the quantitative features used by the ranker. Token assessments and feature attribution lists originate from TreeSHAP Lundberg & Lee (2017); Lundberg et al. (2020) decomposition of the rankers output, while geometric assertions are computed from the same underlying vision features. Training via Distillation Filtering. We adopt Qwen2.5-VL-7B Bai et al. (2025) as the explainer MLLM, using the same base model as teacher to draft explanations for training images. To build high-quality dataset, drafts must pass four distillation filters: Silence Filter discarding geometric claims without valid subject masks, Consistency Filter rejecting values or directions conflicting 22 Preprint. At inference, the explainer receives the input image, the final cropped frame, and structured prompt comprising the four token assessments, frame geometry, and key feature attributions mapped to human-interpretable photographic terms. Anchor sentences derived directly from physical measurements are appended to the prompt to constrain the corresponding statements; they do not guarantee the correctness of the entire generated explanation. IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS View scorer. The view scorer is implemented as hierarchical additive network operating over the 60 standardized features. Each feature is processed by an individual subnetwork (1 32 16 1 with ELU activation), supplemented by pair subnetworks (2 16 8 1) for 20 selected feature pairs. To ensure exact score additive decomposition, each feature output is scaled by learned token weight, with pairwise terms split equally between the tokens of their constituent features. The architecture contains 4.0 104 parameters and is trained on the GAICD training set using withinimage pairwise ranking loss, applied to crop pairs from the same image with MOS differences of at least 0.1. Optimization employs Adam (learning rate 103, weight decay 105, pair batch size 8,192) with early stopping based on validation SRCC (patience 15), where the optimal checkpoint is selected at epoch 60. Ranker. Training uses learning rate of 0.05. The model combines three component scores qA (0.6 regression / 0.4 ranking), qB (0.55 / 0.45), and qC (0.6 / 0.4) with isotonic calibration into final score = 0.4qA + 0.4qB + 0.2qC, totaling approximately 2.1 104 parameters.
